risk_rationale: PCE inflation re-accelerated to 3.6% YoY (+23bp vs prior snapshot) while Core PCE holds at 3.1%, materially above the Fed's 2% target and closing off any near-term easing path. A WTI crude drop of $4.52 to $103.37 provides modest relief on energy costs but Brent at $123.1 signals persistent global supply tightness that threatens to reignite headline inflation. The combination of sticky services inflation, elevated energy prices, and a 37bp positively-sloped curve suggests the market is pricing residual rate risk rather than a soft landing.
outlook_headline: Inflation re-acceleration and an oil market in structural supply deficit keep the Fed cornered and risk assets on a short leash.
outlook_body: The macro backdrop is increasingly hostile for duration and risk assets simultaneously: PCE YoY is moving in the wrong direction at 3.6%, Core PCE at 3.1% is over 100bp above target, and real GDP running at 3.4% annualized removes any urgency for the Fed to pivot. Labor markets are decelerating — 29K NFP is well below trend — but unemployment at 4.2% and wages at 3.9% YoY are insufficient to bring services inflation to heel quickly. Brent crude at $123.1 represents a clear upside risk to the next CPI and PCE prints, and a saving rate of 3.8% leaves consumers with limited buffer if energy costs re-accelerate. Portfolios should remain defensively positioned with underweights in long duration and HY credit until inflation trajectory shows a credible reversal.

tabs.gdp: Real GDP at 3.4% annualized is robust on the surface but is increasingly dependent on government spending and inventory dynamics that are not durable growth drivers. With NFP at 29K, consumer saving at 3.8%, and energy acting as a consumption tax at current Brent levels, the components necessary to sustain above-trend growth are visibly deteriorating. A deceleration to sub-2% GDP in the next two quarters is the base case risk; stagflation — defined by sub-1% growth alongside PCE above 3.5% — is a non-trivial tail scenario.
tabs.jobs: November's 29K NFP is a sharp deceleration and sits well below the 100K threshold needed to absorb labor force growth, signaling that the labor market is losing momentum faster than the unemployment rate of 4.2% implies. Wages at 3.9% YoY remain elevated enough to sustain services inflation, creating a dangerous stagflationary combination of weakening job creation and sticky wage costs. U-6 at 7.6% — nearly double U-3 — points to significant underemployment slack that will widen as hiring continues to cool.
tabs.unemp: U-3 at 4.2% has risen meaningfully from cycle lows and, combined with U-6 at 7.6%, indicates a 340bp gap that reflects significant underemployment and part-time-for-economic-reasons pressure. The U-6 spread of 340bp above U-3 is wide and signals that labor market slack is broader than the headline rate conveys. If NFP remains near 29K, U-3 will breach 4.5% within two to three months — a threshold that historically accelerates Fed dovish pivots.
tabs.wages: Wage growth at 3.9% YoY is nominal; with CPI at 3.7%, real wage growth is essentially flat at approximately +0.2%, providing minimal incremental consumer purchasing power. While 3.9% wage growth is not itself inflationary at the Fed's target, it remains inconsistent with a sustainable return to 2% PCE given services inflation stickiness. The oil price spike risks eroding even this thin real wage buffer, squeezing household cash flow in Q4.
tabs.cpi: Headline CPI at 3.7% YoY is running nearly double the Fed's implicit tolerance, and the $5.98 WTI move guarantees upward pressure on November and December CPI prints before base effects can help. Core CPI at 2.6% is more contained but remains above target; the risk is that energy pass-through to core services re-widens the gap between headline and core. This print sequence removes any near-term probability of Fed easing and may force a hawkish hold with a tightening bias reinstated.
tabs.pce: PCE YoY rose 23bp to 3.65% in the latest reading, a directionally alarming move that confirms inflation is not on a linear path to target. Core PCE at 3.1% is particularly concerning as it strips out the volatile components that would otherwise explain the re-acceleration, pointing to entrenched services and shelter inflation. A household saving rate of 3.8% is thin and leaves consumers exposed to any further energy or credit cost increases, raising the risk of an abrupt consumption pullback.
tabs.yield: The 10Y at 4.98% and 2Y at 4.61% produce a 37bp positive slope — a curve that has steepened on growth resilience rather than Fed easing expectations, leaving no safe haven in duration. With PCE YoY ticking up to 3.6% and Core PCE at 3.1%, the Fed at 3.88% remains in negative real short-rate territory on a PCE basis, sustaining a hawkish bias. A move toward 5.25% on the 10Y cannot be dismissed if the next two inflation prints fail to decelerate.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 89bp and HY OAS at 326bp reflect a market that is complacent relative to the macro signals — spreads at these levels price a benign credit cycle that a 29K NFP print and rising PCE do not support. HY at 326bp offers insufficient compensation for late-cycle default risk, particularly in energy-cost-sensitive issuers and leveraged consumer-facing sectors. A credit spread widening event is a high-conviction risk in this environment; reduce HY exposure and favor IG short duration.
tabs.housing: The 30-year mortgage at 7.24% continues to freeze existing homeowners in place and compress new purchase demand, but Housing Starts at 1,221K suggest builders are sustaining supply at levels that will pressure new home prices. Affordability remains near historic lows with the 10Y at 4.98% providing no relief catalyst for mortgage rates in the near term. Any sustained move in the 10Y toward 5.25%+ would likely push the 30Y mortgage above 7.5%, further locking transaction volume and threatening homebuilder earnings visibility.
tabs.oil: WTI pulled back $4.52 to $103.37 in the latest snapshot, but the $19.73 Brent-WTI spread at $123.1 Brent is anomalously wide and signals acute global supply constraints that the WTI decline does not resolve. At these Brent levels, energy is a direct tax on corporate margins and consumer disposable income, and any supply disruption could push WTI back above $108. The energy complex remains a primary upside risk to PCE and CPI trajectory — this WTI dip should not be read as a structural relief signal.
tabs.banks: Net interest income faces compression as deposit repricing catches up to asset yields, and the 37bp curve — while positive — is too flat to generate meaningful NIM expansion for most bank business models. Credit quality is a growing concern: CC delinquency at 2.9% is trending in the wrong direction alongside a labor market generating only 29K jobs per month, and HY exposure on bank balance sheets carries spread widening risk. Banks with heavy consumer lending books and significant CRE exposure should be treated with caution; favor capital-markets-heavy franchises with fee income diversification.

signal_flags.note: Inflation re-acceleration closes the door on Fed easing and raises the risk of an additional hike; directional move is more important than the absolute level.

Single-snapshot decline does not change the structural supply story; Brent at $123.1 with a $19.73 spread signals global tightness that will sustain inflation pressure — do not treat WTI pullback as a relief signal.
Brent at $123.1 represents a direct upside risk to next PCE/CPI prints; a supply disruption of any magnitude could rapidly reignite headline inflation above 4%.
Below any reasonable full-employment threshold; signals labor market deterioration that will lag into unemployment and consumer spending data within 2-3 months.
Over 100bp above target with no clear momentum toward 2%; services inflation embedded in this reading is not oil-price-dependent and will be slow to resolve.
Rising delinquency alongside decelerating job growth is an early-stage consumer credit stress signal; monitor for acceleration toward 3.5% as a portfolio risk trigger.
Approaching the psychologically and technically significant 5% level; a breach would likely trigger duration selling and spread widening across risk assets.
